F̄d = ½mv²: longer stopping distance means lower average force.
Peaks can be about twice the average or spike when padding bottoms out; stress also depends on contact area.
ω = rpm × 2π/60; inward aᵣ = ω²r; RCF conventionally denotes aᵣ/g, a ratio rather than a force.
Disk I = ½MR²; KE = ½Iω²; L = Iω; τ = Iα.
Unbalanced force Δm ω² r rotates with the rotor; balance by mass, symmetrically.
RCF ∝ ω²r; KE ∝ ω²: twice the speed stores four times the energy.
Differentiate each position component; speed is the magnitude of velocity.
Solve the specified final-height equation and retain roots in the declared interval.
Constant-velocity frames change velocity but preserve acceleration under the stated Galilean model.
Endpoint positions do not uniquely determine intervening instantaneous acceleration.
List forces acting on the chosen body; third-law partners act on different bodies.
Use the friction required for equilibrium and check it does not exceed μ_sN.
Normal contact cannot pull in the simple unilateral-contact model; reassess a negative calculated normal.
Contact forces contribute to net force together with weight and other interactions.
Internal collision forces cancel for total momentum; translational kinetic energy need not be conserved.
Impulse integrates force over time; work integrates its component along displacement.
Time and displacement averages differ and neither uniquely identifies a peak force.
Use net force balance before interpreting momentum change as a contact load.
Use r×F about a declared origin and mass distribution about the specified rotation axis.
No-slip rolling includes center translation and rotation; static friction must support the constraint.
Scalar L=Iω is limited to the stated axis/symmetry conditions.
Ideal static contact on a fixed surface has zero local contact-point velocity; a moving support changes the power analysis.
ω₀=√(k/m),δ=c/(2m) and ω_d=√(ω₀²−δ²) apply to the stated underdamped model.
Mechanical energy decreases at rate cv²; integrate this loss to check the energy ledger.
The sine coefficient must satisfy the initial derivative when an exponential envelope is present.
A period constrains parameter combinations; more independent observations are needed to recover damping and stiffness.
Use initial area and gauge length for engineering stress and strain; state how modulus is defined.
σ=Eε+ηε′ combines elastic and rate terms in the supplied scalar model.
Crosshead motion can include machine and grip deformation or slip beyond specimen extension.
Record orientation, geometry, hydration, temperature, rate, history and modulus definition before comparing material values.
An additive displacement offset changes the intercept; series compliance changes the force slope.
Subtract independently known machine compliance from total compliance and invert after consistent unit conversion.
Measured reference slope includes reference compliance unless that contribution is stipulated zero or corrected.
A residual orientation contrast under matched conditions does not uniquely identify a microscopic tissue mechanism.
Subtracting a constant zero-force offset leaves force-dependent machine compliance.
Subtract independently estimated machine compliance from total compliance, then invert in consistent units.
A finite-compliance reference needs its independently known compliance removed from its observed slope.
Matched corrected stiffnesses support a conditional contrast; they do not uniquely identify a real tissue mechanism.
d(mv)/dt = Fext + Σin mdot w − Σout mdot w, with positive rate magnitudes and stream velocities in one inertial frame.
For backward relative exhaust speed u>0 and rocket mass loss mdot<0: m dv/dt = Fext − u mdot = Fext + u q, where q=−mdot>0.
With constant relative exhaust speed and negligible external force, Δv = u ln(m0/mf); it is an ideal velocity increment, not a complete real-vehicle prediction.
Incoming material contributes its inertial-frame momentum; a moving body that captures material initially at rest slows if external impulse is negligible.
F = Gm₁m₂/r², r between centres (shell result for spheres). g = GM/R² is local; at r = 2R it is a quarter.
GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), independent of the satellite's mass; T² = 4π²r³/GM.
U = −GMm/r with zero at infinity; ΔU = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂), which reduces to mgh only for h ≪ r.
Circular orbit: K = GMm/(2r), E = −GMm/(2r). Escape speed √(2GM/r) is √2 times the circular speed at the same radius.
ω = √(target × g/r): at the same acceleration ratio, a smaller sample radius needs a higher angular speed, by √2 when the radius halves.

cards.front: Disk energy at a fixed target
cards.back: For a uniform disk with the sample at its rim, K = ½(½MR²)ω² = ¼ M R × target × g, so energy grows with both mass and radius.
A point imbalance m at the sample radius needs m ω² r = m × target × g of inward force, and the support carries the matching rotating load in this ideal model.

cards.front: Why can a light rope have different tensions on opposite sides of a massive pulley?
cards.back: Rim interaction transmits net torque to accelerate the pulley; equal tension across it would contradict nonzero rotational acceleration.

cards.front: Which energy terms belong in a massive-pulley calculation?
cards.back: Both mass translations and pulley rotation, along with the potential change and any separately supplied losses.
Consistency with the declared equations in a controlled limit; they do not validate omitted traction, deformation or real support behavior.

cards.front: Why record a stopping event in a model report?
cards.back: A valid phase solution can become invalid when contact, tautness or another constraint changes; a numerical continuation must specify the new model.

cards.front: Which velocity determines kinetic friction direction?
cards.back: The relative velocity at the contact point, v−R omega in the stated signs; it need not have the same sign as center velocity.

cards.front: Why does friction times center displacement overcount loss during spin-up?
cards.back: Some translational energy is transferred into rotation; total mechanical power uses the actual force-application-point velocity.

cards.front: Can friction increase center speed while decreasing total mechanical energy?
cards.back: Yes. It can reduce excess spin and accelerate translation while opposing relative contact slip.

cards.front: What must an event-aware contact simulation preserve?
cards.back: The sign and magnitude rules within each phase, a correctly located zero-slip event and a post-event constraint/force law consistent with the new state.

cards.front: What distinguishes an open-body momentum balance from fixed-mass F=ma?
cards.back: It includes the momentum carried by incoming/outgoing material, with velocities and the system boundary defined in a common frame.

cards.front: Why is external work insufficient to infer the final kinetic energy of a capturing body?
cards.back: Incoming/outgoing kinetic energy and mechanical loss can enter; track the complete energy ledger for the declared mass flow.

cards.front: What should a constrained-motion report retain beyond its solved values?
cards.back: Original signed force/torque equations, explicit geometric constraints, residuals, energy and limiting-case checks, and the phase’s validity interval.

cards.front: What changes at a hard stop in a constrained-motion calculation?
cards.back: The active contact and rope constraints may change; end the valid pre-impact solution and state any assumptions for continuation.

cards.front: Why compare both an event time and energy loss in contact verification?
cards.back: They test different consequences of the phase dynamics; an apparently correct endpoint speed can conceal an incorrect contact-force history.

cards.front: Does independence of final rolling speed from kinetic mu imply independence of transition time?
cards.back: No. In this ideal model, final speed follows a coupled invariant while event time scales inversely with positive mu.

cards.front: Why verify a numerical oscillator against both a trajectory and an energy identity?
cards.back: Phase, amplitude and energy errors can differ; an exact mechanical law and analytic reference expose artifacts that a smooth graph can hide.

cards.front: Does a one-step numerical energy decrease prove physical damping?
cards.back: No. The mechanical law specifies damping; numerical integrators can alter computed energy even when the exact model conserves it.
